newsitem.title: HONG KONG: PLA's Hong Kong entry stirs end-of-empire quarrel.
newsitem.headline: PLA's Hong Kong entry stirs end-of-empire quarrel.

text.p: China's imminent large-scale military entry into Hong Kong has stirred up a new end-of-empire quarrel with the departing British administration, but military experts regard it as a storm in a teacup.

China announced on Friday it would send in 4,000 troops of its People's Liberation Army (PLA) by land, sea and air at dawn on Tuesday, six hours after Britain's midnight Monday (1600 GMT) withdrawal brings 156 years of colonial rule to an end.
This will bring PLA strength in Hong Kong to about 4,700, with 196 already here as an advance party and 509 due three hours before the change of flag.
The troops, with helicopters, ships, 21 armoured cars and 400 other vehicles, will cross the northern border at three points.

"It doesn't sound to me the right sort of signal to send to the international community and above all I think it is a most appalling signal to send to the people of Hong Kong," declared British Governor Chris Patten.
In London the Foreign Office said China was sending out negative signals. Hong Kong's pro-democracy lobby was outraged.

"The Chinese want to end their 'century of humiliation' in grand style, but they should show more sensitivity towards Hong Kong people's feelings. Hong Kong people are not enamoured of the PLA," said legislator Emily Lau, a voice of democracy.
"They like to act the bully. They should have come in a more low-key fashion."

The departing British garrison chief, Major-General Bryan Dutton, has said more than once recently that the PLA garrison will be the most important demonstration of sovereignty for the Chinese, after a century and a half of British rule.
A Western military attache said the impact of the PLA's arrival should not be exaggerated. "They've never been going to come in dribs and drabs," he said.

Another military analyst said: "The political fuss is overplayed. It's just the political game of the departing colonial power with wounded pride versus the triumphalist Chinese, rubbing their hands with glee and restoring their own pride and sovereignty."
A western military source said the PLA would bring four missile patrol boats weighing 750 tonnes each, equivalent to the Peacock class patrol vessels that Britain had stationed here.
They would bring three medium landing craft big enough to handle a 100-man company of soldiers, two catamarans for use between islands and small police-style patrol boats.
The troops were expected to bring in Z-9 helicopters modelled on the French Dauphine. Britain kept a squadron of six Wessex helicopters in Hong Kong in its latter days.
In recent years, however, the British military was not known to keep armoured cars in the territory.

The armoured cars struck a particularly raw nerve in Hong Kong, which remembers with horror similar vehicles being used to crush pro-democracy protest in Tiananmen Square in June, 1989. A million Hong Kongers took to the streets to protest the massacre and capital took flight from the territory's coffers.

Some people also worry that the Chinese garrison will answer directly to Beijing and not to Hong Kong leader Tung Chee-hwa -- unlike the situation with the British army, which was controlled by the governor.

The PLA launched a charm blitz early this year, inviting Hong Kong media into China to watch them train. The generals have stressed they are an elite corps with high prowess, discipline and intellect.

Hong Kong's future constitution, the Basic Law, promulgated by China, says Beijing will be responsible for foreign affairs and defence in post-handover Hong Kong, but the local government will be in charge of all other affairs including public order.
It says troops stationed in Hong Kong will not interfere in local affairs.

It adds, however: "The government of the Hong Kong SAR may, in times of need, ask the Central People's Government for assistance from the garrison in the maintenance of public order and disaster relief."
